title: Choosing sidemen and what makes a musician get called back
summary: Sands keeps a pool of drummers and bassists by rehearsal needs; professionalism and being easy to work with matter more than talent.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Do you have a drummer list, a bass player list, and you line up gigs and a tour and you’ve got to figure out who’s available?

Yeah I mean you have your main guys that you always use, you know, and then you have the guys that if they’re not available who also — it’s not even also it is a substitute because they also are equally as good. It’s just you have your people that you know that you don’t have to rehearse with, they just know the music and then you know it’s less work for you to do on that side of it. So those are the guys. And then you have the ones like okay if we do one rehearsal they’ll be fine. You know, cool. And then you have the guys like okay if we do two rehearsals that will be fine. And then you know you just keep going and going and going. You know. But yeah, there’s always a set of people that you kind of have, but then you also learn about other people. You learn about new people and

then you try to figure out okay where can I put this now because I really want to play with this person now. But now this person is used to me calling him all the time so how do we do that? When do we do that? Or just call them both. And now you just have a double trio or something like that. You know? Options.
What would cause you to not call somebody back that, even though they might be a really good player? Is there anything that sort of irks you?

I mean if they’re just not professional, you know? Like if anyone is just unprofessional or you know just not a nice person. I mean you’d be surprised — you can be the most talented person in the world but if no one likes you they won’t call you. You know. Like if you’re not easy to work with or there’s always a thing then it’s not going to work out. And you can be like the fifth most talented person in the room or so, and if you’re easy to work — and you come correct, and you come with all your music ready and like everything is in place and professional, you’ll get so many more gigs like that. And then you also learn on the bandstand to be better and better and better and better and better. So you know, that’s kind of how I see it.
